title: A repeat hearing test
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on the postnatal ward. Baby Lily, two days old, had her newborn hearing screen this morning. It didn't show a clear response in one ear, and the screener has arranged a second test before discharge.

Lily's parents stop you as you pass. They are anxious and ask you whether this means she is deaf.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 4 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Offer to ask the screener to come and talk to them about the second test.
options.brief: The screener can give detailed information and answer their questions.
options.detailed: The screener knows the test well and can explain exactly what will happen. Arranging this is helpful; it ranks second because the parents are anxious now, and you can give them accurate information straight away.

options.text: Tell them the screener will explain everything at the second test.
options.brief: Not wrong, but leaves them worrying until then.
options.detailed: The screener will explain the test, but the parents are anxious now. Putting them off when you could give them some accurate information misses an opportunity to help.

options.text: Explain that a second test is common and doesn't necessarily mean hearing loss.
options.brief: Honest, accurate information is reassuring without making promises.
options.detailed: It's common for newborns not to give a clear response on the first test, often because of fluid or a temporary blockage in the ear, background noise, or the baby being unsettled. Most babies who need a second test don't have permanent hearing loss. Explaining this honestly, without promising a result, gives the parents real reassurance.

options.text: Reassure them that you are sure Lily's hearing will turn out to be completely normal.
options.brief: Kind, but makes a promise you can't keep.
options.detailed: This is tempting, as you want to relieve their worry. But you can't know the result, and if Lily does have a hearing problem, false reassurance would damage their trust.

explanation.issue: This tests how you communicate uncertainty to anxious parents: honestly, accurately, and without false reassurance.
explanation.keyDetails: A second test is common and doesn't necessarily mean hearing loss. The parents are anxious now. You can't know the result.
explanation.reasoning: [C] gives accurate, honest reassurance, and [A] arranges more detailed information. [B] defers when you could help, and [D] makes a promise you can't keep.
explanation.competing: Some would rank deferral last, since it doesn't help at all. The key puts false reassurance last because it could damage their trust if Lily does have a hearing problem.

references.title: Screening tests for you and your baby: hearing loss
references.note: A second test doesn't necessarily mean hearing loss; common reasons include fluid in the ear and an unsettled baby.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 2, giving patients and families honest information.
